option_rationales.rationale: Argument III is also strong; reducing manual cash handling is a direct operational gain.

common_traps: Accepting an argument that overgeneralises ('majority will switch') as strong.

short_explanation: The passage says economic constraints often prevent investment in human capital in Africa (II) and that helping Africa means investing in local leadership, who hold the keys to progress (I). III contradicts this.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Leaves out II; the passage states that tight economic constraints hold back investment in education.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Leaves out I; the passage stresses engaging local leaders.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: III contradicts the passage, which gives local leaders a key role.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: III contradicts the passage.

common_traps: Rejecting II because 'hampered the growth' is not word for word; 'prevent sustained investment' carries the same meaning.

short_explanation: Medicine and dentistry graduates earn about £47,300, above the £27,600 average (I). Teaching-degree graduates earn slightly less than law graduates at £25,200, so below the average (II). III fails because the list covers only 20 courses.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Leaves out II; teaching graduates earn less than £25,200, which is under the £27,600 average.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Leaves out I, which follows directly from £47,300 exceeding £27,600.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: III does not follow; only 20 courses were ranked, so others may also earn above the average.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: III does not follow, so not all three do.

key_note: Accepted as defensible. Statement II speaks of 'teachers' generally, while the passage covers teaching-degree graduates five years after university; the key reads the two as the same group.

short_explanation: Department G's machines break down from overuse while Department K's sit underused. Moving workers from G to K spreads the work to the idle machines, which fits the HR head's role (II). Buying new machinery is a costly step outside her remit and ignores the spare capacity in K (I).

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Course I ignores the idle capacity in Department K and is a capital decision beyond the HR head's role.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The two courses are not alternatives; only II follows.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: II follows, since it uses K's idle machines and eases the load in G.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: I does not follow, so both cannot.

common_traps: Choosing new machinery because it fixes G, without seeing the unused capacity already available in K.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. Another reading set aside: Course I (new machinery for G) could also be seen as practical, but it overlooks K's spare capacity and goes beyond an HR head's authority, which is why the key rejects it.

short_explanation: The company expects its online move for electronics to succeed the way clothing did, which only makes sense if digitally literate clients will also want electronic goods.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Not assumed; the plan does not depend on rivals having no online presence.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Not assumed; the passage says nothing about reusing the same designer.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Not assumed; other companies' designers are irrelevant to the plan.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Not assumed; the passage says nothing about closing the physical business.

common_traps: Picking the designer option because the web designer is mentioned; the plan's success hinges on the customers, not the designer.

short_explanation: The bee had not been seen for nearly 40 years despite its large size, and it was rediscovered in a remote area. This supports that earlier attempts to find it failed (I). Conservation (II) and adaptation (III) are not mentioned.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: III is speculation; the passage gives no information on how the bee adapted.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: II does not follow; the passage says nothing about conservation efforts.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: II does not follow; conservation is never mentioned.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: III does not follow; adaptation is not discussed.

key_note: Accepted as defensible. Conclusion I goes slightly beyond the text, since the passage does not mention expeditions; it is accepted because 'no one had observed' a conspicuous bee implies that earlier searches failed.

short_explanation: The passage calls 'the centerpiece' of the plan 'a novel plant vaccine derived from harmless protein fragments that train plant immunity to recognize common viral and fungal signatures'. Option a restates this, with 'non-pathogenic' for 'harmless'.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: The vaccine trains plant immunity; the passage never says it alters plant genetic structures.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Chemical pesticides and mechanical tools are not mentioned; termites are handled with root-zone barriers and odour cues.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The passage links moisture to fungal outbreaks and advises airflow; it does not suggest retaining moisture.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Soil health is one part of the plan, but no new soil additive is described, and it is not the centrepiece.

common_traps: Choosing b because 'long-term immunity' sounds like a vaccine; the passage says the fragments train immunity, not that they change genes.

short_explanation: The passage says the report 'shows why early rains, dense planting, and poor air circulation often set the stage for outbreaks'. Option c restates these three conditions.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Chlorophyll and potassium build-up is never mentioned.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Monoculture and crop diversification are never mentioned.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Fertiliser use and nitrogen saturation are never mentioned.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: The passage does not link higher fruit yield to termites; termites target cellulose.

common_traps: Picking an option that sounds agriculturally sensible but is not in the passage; the answer must come from the text.

short_explanation: The passage says 'Rapid mutation allows viruses' to get past plant defences, 'Fungi swap genetic material through spores', and 'Termite colonies reorganize quickly'. All three change fast, each by a different route.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The passage says viruses mutate rapidly, so they do alter; external vectors are not mentioned.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Fungi are not stable; they 'swap genetic material through spores'.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Termite colonies are not static; they 'reorganize quickly, shifting attack sites'.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Fungi and termites also adapt quickly, so it is not only viruses.

common_traps: Taking 'mutation' literally and choosing e; the passage describes adaptation for all three, only by different means.

short_explanation: Only statement III is supported: the passage names 'early rains, dense planting, and poor air circulation' as conditions that set the stage for outbreaks.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I is false: the vaccine trains plant immunity; it does not raise sugar content.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Both I and II are false; II invents recombination for viruses and protein mimicry for termites.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I is false, so this pair fails.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Statements I and II are false.

common_traps: Accepting II because 'genetic' appears in the passage; it is fungi that swap genetic material, and viruses are said to mutate.

short_explanation: The closing guidance says 'Space rows for airflow, prune regularly' (statement I) and 'Use the vaccine at the seedling stage and repeat before peak humidity' (statement III). Chemical insecticides (statement II) are never advised.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Leaves out III, which the passage advises directly.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes II; the passage never recommends chemical insecticides.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Leaves out I, which the passage advises directly.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: II is not advised, so all three cannot be right.

common_traps: Assuming a pest-control plan must include insecticides; the plan relies on hygiene, soil health and biological control.

short_explanation: 'Each sample was placed in controlled conditions' means each sample was carefully put or set in a controlled setting. 'Positioned' carries that sense of deliberate placing.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 'Thrown' suggests careless force, not careful lab handling.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 'Dropped' suggests letting something fall, not setting it in place.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 'Tossed' suggests a casual throw, which does not fit careful lab work.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'Floated' means resting on liquid, which the passage does not describe.

short_explanation: In 'even low-level infections can spoil harvest timing and market quality', 'spoil' means damage or ruin. 'Ruin' is the closest synonym.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 'Enhance' means improve, the opposite of the meaning here.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 'Ferment' is a literal chemical change in food, not the sense of damaging timing and quality.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 'Delay' could fit timing, but it cannot describe damage to market quality; 'spoil' means ruin, not postpone.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'Expand' means enlarge, which makes no sense here.

common_traps: Choosing 'delay' because 'harvest timing' is mentioned; the word must also cover 'market quality', so the meaning is 'ruin'.

short_explanation: The paragraph is about how quickly the enemies of plants adapt, and the next sentences describe spreading and shifting attack sites. 'Rapid mutation allows viruses to dodge plant defenses' means mutation helps viruses escape those defences.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 'To harden plant defenses' would mean the viruses strengthen the plant, which is the opposite of the point.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 'To support plant defenses' likewise helps the plant, which contradicts the threat described.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 'To transmit plant defenses' is meaningless; viruses do not pass on a plant's defences.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'To nourish plant defenses' would help the plant, contradicting the threat described.

short_explanation: 'Condone' means to accept or overlook behaviour that is wrong. Sentences I and III use it correctly (refusing to excuse cheating; a light sentence seen as excusing a crime). Sentence II misuses it for adding spices to a recipe.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Leaves out sentence III, which correctly uses 'condoned' for excusing the criminal's actions.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Sentence II is the wrong use; the writer means 'seasoned' or 'spiced up'.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes sentence II, the wrong use, and leaves out sentence I.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Sentence II misuses the word, so not all are correct.

common_traps: Confusing 'condone' with 'condiment' because of the similar sound.

short_explanation: Only sentence B is correct. A needs 'is still suffering from'; C needs 'The platform economy' and 'assures' to agree with the singular subject; D needs 'aimed to advance' or 'aimed at advancing'.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Sentence A is wrong: 'is still suffered from' should be 'is still suffering from'.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Sentence C is wrong: 'promotes ... and assure' should be 'promotes ... and assures'.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: A, C and D all contain errors, and the correct B is left out.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Both A and C contain errors.

common_traps: Letting 'aimed at advance' pass; after 'at' the verb takes the -ing form ('advancing').

short_explanation: A, C and D are incorrect. A: 'archives' is plural, so 'were opened'. C: 'The book comprises essays that explore'. D: 'insisted on attending', since 'insist' takes 'on' with an -ing form, not 'to'. B is correct.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Sentence B is correct, and C and D, which have errors, are left out.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Leaves out A and D, which also have errors.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: B is the one correct sentence, not an incorrect one.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Leaves out D ('insisted to attend'), which is also wrong.

common_traps: Matching the verb to 'museum' in A instead of to the plural head noun 'archives'.

short_explanation: The Citations were 'built ... to ferry corporate executives cross-country', meaning built to carry them. 'Built for the movement corporate executives' lacks 'of' and is clumsy.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 'in order to transport a corporate executives' puts the singular article 'a' before the plural 'executives'.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 'for the part of corporate executives' makes no sense.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The printed phrase lacks 'of' ('the movement of'), so a replacement is needed.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'sleek and classy where corporate executives' breaks the sentence and leaves 'built' without a purpose.

common_traps: Choosing a because 'transport' is the right idea; the stray article 'a' makes it ungrammatical.

short_explanation: Windscreens 'filmed over with dust' means covered by a thin layer of dust, which suits abandoned aircraft. 'Gliding with dust' makes no sense.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 'feeling bloated with dust' gives windscreens a feeling, which does not fit.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 'gliding with dust' is meaningless, so a replacement is needed.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 'completely goaded with dust' misuses 'goad', which means to provoke.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'that have coated with dust' needs the passive 'that have been coated'; as given, the windscreens do the coating.

common_traps: Choosing e for its sense of coating; the active 'have coated' is the wrong voice.

short_explanation: 'As if nature were prying them back from human hands' is already correct: 'were' is the subjunctive used after 'as if', and 'prying back from' means forcing them away, which fits weeds pushing up through the wheel bays.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 'intends to give these away from human hands' is ungrammatical and reverses the meaning.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 'has snatched it from from human hands' repeats 'from', and 'it' does not match the plural aircraft.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 'was prying with from human hands' is ungrammatical and drops the subjunctive 'were'.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'strongly dislikes the ones from human hands' is meaningless here.

common_traps: Replacing 'were' with 'was' after 'as if'; the subjunctive 'were' is correct for an imagined situation.

short_explanation: 'In some corners, forest has crept in, swallowing the outlines of these grounded giants in leaves and shadow' completes the image: the growth slowly covers the aircraft. 'Has become dense, outside of' makes no sense with 'in leaves and shadow'.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 'has show up' is ungrammatical ('has shown up'), and 'despite the skeleton these grounded giants' makes no sense.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 'taken roots' should be 'taken root', and 'the boundary that these grounded giants in leaves' has no verb.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 'covering each these grounded giants' is ungrammatical; 'each' cannot go with 'these'.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'has become dense, outside of these grounded giants in leaves and shadow' is meaningless, so a replacement is needed.

common_traps: Choosing c for its sense of covering; 'each these' is ungrammatical.

short_explanation: The writer is playing on the idiom 'go the way of all flesh' (to die). 'Where aircraft come to spend their final days' keeps the sentence grammatical after 'come to' and fits the image of a graveyard where retired planes rest.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 'And joint the choir' is not English here; 'joint' is not a verb and 'come to and join' breaks the sentence.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: After 'come to' we need a base verb, so 'come to dying in peace' is ungrammatical.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 'Meet death by misfortune' suggests crashes or accidents, but these planes are simply retired and parked, not destroyed by bad luck.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'Take the way of all mechanics' is a garbled version of the idiom 'go the way of all flesh' and makes no sense as written, so a replacement is needed.

common_traps: Candidates pick 'meet death' because 'graveyard' suggests death, but the passage describes planes that are retired and stored, not wrecked.

short_explanation: The sentence contrasts how boneyards look ('they might look like mechanical cemeteries') with what they really are, so it needs a verb plus a noun phrase: 'they are also valuable treasure troves for a vast, little-known industry'.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 'They be anything less than' has no proper verb form for 'they'; the idea would need 'they are anything but'.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 'They appears' breaks subject-verb agreement, and 'nothing short' needs 'of' before 'treasure troves'.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 'May at least as a' has no main verb and leaves the sentence broken.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'They have immense importance for treasure troves' makes the boneyards important to treasure troves, when the point is that the boneyards themselves are treasure troves.

common_traps: Reading only the words right after the highlight: 'treasure troves' is the complement, so the replacement must supply 'are' and connect to it directly.

short_explanation: Four sentences are about feedback to students in education: constructive feedback, timely responses from instructors, peer review and personalized comments on assignments. Option d moves to 'feedback in the workplace' and 'employee retention', which is a different setting.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Stays on the theme: feedback that helps students see strengths and weaknesses.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Stays on the theme: instructors' timely responses and student motivation.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Stays on the theme: peer review is feedback among students.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Stays on the theme: personalized comments link students and educators.

common_traps: The word 'feedback' appears in option d too, so a quick keyword scan misses that its setting (employees, not students) is different.

short_explanation: The other four sentences list benefits of urban green spaces: well-being, cleaner air, planning priority and lower stress. Option b says some green spaces are mainly used for commercial festivals and private events, which does not support that theme of public benefit.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Fits: green spaces support mental and physical well-being.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Fits: trees reduce pollution and heat, another benefit.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Fits: planners value green infrastructure for sustainable cities.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Fits: parks lower stress and increase community interaction.

common_traps: Option d looks different because it talks about planners, not residents, but it still supports the value of green spaces.

short_explanation: Swapping 'refining' and 'adjusting' gives 'The artist kept adjusting the painting and refining the lighting in the studio', which is still grammatical and sensible, since both words are verbs in '-ing' form that suit both objects.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping 'lighting' and 'refining' gives 'kept lighting the painting and adjusting the refining', which makes no sense.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping 'adjusting' and 'lighting' gives 'kept refining the painting and lighting the adjusting', which makes no sense.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Neither A with C nor B with C works, because 'lighting' here is a noun (the object), not a matching action.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: One swap, 'refining' with 'adjusting', does work, so 'no swapping possible' is wrong.

common_traps: 'Lighting' ends in '-ing' like the verbs, but here it is a noun meaning the lamps and light in the studio, so it cannot trade places with them.

short_explanation: None of the swaps works: 'struggling through' the phases, 'trying different combinations' and 'combinations' as the object each need their own place, so no other sequence keeps the sentence meaningful.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping gives 'Despite trying through the initial phases... the scientist kept struggling different combinations'; 'struggling combinations' is not English.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping gives 'Despite combinations through the initial phases... kept trying struggling'; a noun cannot follow 'despite' in that role here.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping gives 'kept combinations trying different', which breaks the verb-object order.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Both of the listed swaps fail, as shown for options b and c.

common_traps: 'Struggling' and 'trying' are both '-ing' verbs, which tempts a swap, but 'struggle' needs 'through' or 'with' and cannot take 'different combinations' as its object.

short_explanation: Swapping 'planning' and 'organizing' gives 'After organizing the event for months and planning with multiple teams', which still reads well because both verbs suit both phrases.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping 'planning' and 'executed everything' gives 'After executed everything the event for months', which is ungrammatical.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping 'organizing' and 'executed everything' breaks both clauses.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Neither A with C nor B with C works; the main verb 'executed' cannot move into the 'after' phrase.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: The swap of 'planning' and 'organizing' works, so 'no swapping possible' is wrong.

common_traps: Only words of the same form can swap; 'executed' is the main past-tense verb of the sentence, while 'planning' and 'organizing' are '-ing' forms after 'after'.

short_explanation: The story runs in time order: Mira researched weaving patterns before the meeting (B), drafted interview questions (A), noticed changes in the motifs during the interview (D), and the published article came last (C). So the order is B A D C.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Starts with drafting questions, but B says 'Before meeting the artisan' she researched, which should open the account.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Puts the interview (D) before drafting questions (A), but questions are prepared before an interview.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Opens with 'During the interview', yet research and preparation must come first.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Puts the interview before the research that B says came 'before meeting the artisan'.

common_traps: Both A and B are preparation steps; the phrase 'Before meeting the artisan' marks B as the very first step.

short_explanation: 'Come down on' someone means to punish or criticise them severely. 'Take action against' keeps that meaning, but 'let on the secret to' (reveal a secret) and 'ignore the mistake of' (the opposite idea) cannot replace it, so B and C are the ones that fail.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: A can replace the bold part, so 'Only A' wrongly names a valid phrase as invalid.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes A, which fits, and leaves out C, which does not.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Leaves out B, which also cannot replace the bold part.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: A does fit ('threatened to take action against the employee'), so not all three fail.

common_traps: The question asks which CANNOT replace the bold part; picking the phrase that fits is the most common slip.

short_explanation: 'Cut down on' means to reduce. 'Scale back on' and 'curb the level of' both mean reduce, but 'ramp up' means to increase, the opposite, so only C cannot replace the bold part.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 'Scale back on its carbon emissions' means reduce them, so A fits.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 'Curb the level of its carbon emissions' fits, and B cannot be paired with C as failing.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: A fits, so it cannot be paired with C.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: A and B both fit; only C fails.

common_traps: The question asks for the phrase that CANNOT replace the bold part; 'ramp up' is the opposite of 'cut down on'.

short_explanation: Only sentence B is error-free. A needs 'becoming' after 'with online shopping'; C needs 'shocked' (a feeling) and 'imprisonment' (a noun); D needs 'the rainy season' and 'to enjoy' or 'so as to enjoy', not 'as to enjoy'.
explanation_text: In A, the 'with' + noun + '-ing' pattern describes an accompanying situation, so the verb must be 'becoming'. In C, '-ed' adjectives describe how a person feels (shocked, disappointed) while '-ing' adjectives describe what causes the feeling (a shocking event); 'imprison' is a verb, so the noun 'imprisonment' is needed after 'sudden'. In D, the season needs 'the', and purpose is shown with 'to enjoy' or 'so as to enjoy'.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: A is wrong: 'with online shopping become' should be 'with online shopping becoming'.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: C is wrong: people 'felt shocked', not 'shocking', and 'sudden imprison' should be 'sudden imprisonment'.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: A, C and D all contain errors, as explained.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Both A and C contain errors.

common_traps: 'Felt shocking and disappointed' mixes an '-ing' form with an '-ed' form; the feeling of a person always takes the '-ed' form.

short_explanation: A and D are correct. B has no finite verb: it should read 'Since the scandal erupted last January, the company's shares have lost more than half their value.' C needs 'foreigners who have taken', because 'who' refers to plural 'foreigners'.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: B is wrong: 'the company's shares losing' has no proper main verb.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: B is wrong for the same reason, even though D is correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Both B and C contain errors.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: B and C contain errors, so not all four are correct.

common_traps: In C, 'who has' looks fine until you check what 'who' refers to; the antecedent 'foreigners' is plural, so 'have' is needed.

short_explanation: A and D form a cause-and-effect pair: 'Because the branch closed unexpectedly during heavy rainfall, customers missed deposits, causing delayed salary credits.' A connector such as 'because' or 'as a result' joins them naturally.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: A jammed passbook printer and new locker hours are unrelated events; no connector links them sensibly.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: The closure and a notice on locker hours are not linked as cause and effect or contrast.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Changed locker access hours would not stop customers from making deposits.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: A jammed passbook printer only stops passbook updates; it does not stop deposits, so it does not explain D.

common_traps: B and D both happen at a bank counter, which looks related, but only the branch closure actually prevents deposits.

topic_name: Quadratic equations — root comparison (x vs y)
short_explanation: Equation I gives x = 5 or x = −12; equation II gives y = −7 or y = −12. x = 5 is greater than both values of y, but x = −12 equals one value of y and is less than the other, so no single relation holds.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: x = −12 is not greater than y = −7 or y = −12.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: x = 5 is greater than both values of y.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: x = −12 is less than y = −7, so x ≥ y fails.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: x = 5 is greater than both values of y, so x ≤ y fails.

solution_steps: Equation I: x² + 7x − 60 = 0 factorises as (x + 12)(x − 5) = 0, so x = 5 or x = −12.
Equation II: y² + 19y + 84 = 0 factorises as (y + 7)(y + 12) = 0, so y = −7 or y = −12.
Compare every pair: 5 is greater than −7 and −12; −12 equals −12 but is less than −7.
The comparisons point both ways, so no relation can be established.
formula_used: Roots from factorising: product of roots = c/a, sum of roots = −b/a
common_traps: Moving 60 to the left without changing its sign, which gives x² + 7x + 60 = 0 and no real roots.

topic_name: Quadratic equations — root comparison (x vs y)
short_explanation: Equation I gives x = −3 or x = −3.5; equation II is a perfect square giving y = −3 only. x is either equal to y or less than it, so x ≤ y.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: x = −3 equals y, so x < y does not hold for every pair.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Neither value of x is greater than y = −3.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: x = −3.5 is less than y = −3, so x ≥ y fails.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: A definite relation (x ≤ y) exists, so 'no relation' is wrong.

solution_steps: Equation I: 2x² + 13x + 21 = 0 factorises as (2x + 7)(x + 3) = 0, so x = −3.5 or x = −3.
Equation II: y² + 6y + 9 = (y + 3)² = 0, so y = −3.
x = −3.5 is less than y, and x = −3 equals y.
So x ≤ y.
common_traps: Choosing x < y after seeing −3.5 < −3, and forgetting that the other root of x equals y.

topic_name: Quadratic equations — root comparison (x vs y)
short_explanation: x² = 289 gives x = 17 or x = −17, while y³ = 4913 gives only y = 17 (a cube has a single real cube root). So x is either equal to y or less than it: x ≤ y.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: x = 17 equals y, so x < y does not hold for every value.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Neither value of x exceeds y = 17.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: x = −17 is less than y = 17, so x ≥ y fails.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: A definite relation (x ≤ y) exists.

solution_steps: y³ = 4913 = 17 × 17 × 17, so y = 17 (only one real cube root).
−17 is less than 17, and 17 equals 17.
So x ≤ y.
formula_used: Square root has two signs; a real cube root has one
common_traps: Taking only x = 17 and answering x = y.
Giving y a negative root too; a cube root keeps the sign of the number, so y is only +17.

In decimals: x = 1.29 or −1.40; y = 2 or −1.43.
x is below y = 2 but above y = −1.43, so no relation can be established.

topic_name: Number series — multiplicative and mixed patterns
short_explanation: Reading from the right, each term is multiplied by 2, 4, 8, 16 and then 32 (1 × 2 = 2, 2 × 4 = 8, 8 × 8 = 64, 64 × 16 = 1024). So the first term is 1024 × 32 = 32768.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 3000; the working gives 32768.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 2048 is 1024 × 2, which repeats the smallest multiplier instead of continuing to 32.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 2884; the working gives 32768.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 32000 is only a rounded look-alike; 1024 × 32 is exactly 32768.

solution_steps: Divide each term by the next: 1024 ÷ 64 = 16, 64 ÷ 8 = 8, 8 ÷ 2 = 4, 2 ÷ 1 = 2.
The divisors double as we move left: 2, 4, 8, 16, so the next is 32.
common_traps: Doubling 1024 to get 2048 instead of continuing the doubling multipliers.

short_explanation: Cost of 120 pens = 10p and their selling price = (120 ÷ q) × 12 = 1440 ÷ q, so both p and q are needed. The ratio 4 : 5 alone leaves p = 4k, q = 5k with k unknown, and HCF 3 alone does not fix p and q; together p = 12 and q = 15, giving a loss of 20%.

option_rationales.label: b

option_rationales.label: e

solution_steps: Cost price of 120 pens = (120 ÷ 12) × p = 10p.
Selling price of 120 pens = (120 ÷ q) × 12 = 1440 ÷ q.
Statement II alone: p = 4k, q = 5k, so cost 40k and sale value 288 ÷ k; the answer changes with k.
Both together: numbers in ratio 4 : 5 have HCF equal to k, so k = 3, p = 12, q = 15.
common_traps: Assuming a ratio alone fixes a profit percentage; here p and q enter the formula differently (one multiplies, one divides), so the actual values are needed.

short_explanation: Statement II (4 men and 5 women in 4 days) is exactly half the workforce of Statement I (8 men and 10 women in 2 days), so both give the same single equation. One equation cannot separate a man's rate from a woman's rate, so the time for 6 men cannot be found.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I gives one equation in two unknowns (a man's and a woman's daily work).

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement II gives the same single equation.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Together they are still only one equation, since II is I halved.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Neither statement alone is sufficient.

solution_steps: Let a man do m and a woman do w of the work per day.
Statement I: 2(8m + 10w) = 1, so 8m + 10w = 1/2.
Statement II: 4(4m + 5w) = 1, so 4m + 5w = 1/4, which is Statement I divided by 2.
Only one independent equation, so m cannot be found and the question cannot be answered.
common_traps: Assuming two statements always give two equations; check whether one is a multiple of the other.

short_explanation: All solids are mugs, all mugs are glasses and no glass is water, so no solid is water. Some cups are solids, so those cups can never be water.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Every solid is a mug and every mug is a glass, so all solids are glasses; 'some solids are not glasses' is false.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Nothing links cups to liquid, so 'no cups are liquid' is not certain.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Mugs are glasses and no glass is water, so no mug is water; the conclusion is false.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Solids are linked to liquid only through water, and 'some water is not liquid' gives no fixed relation, so this is not certain.

solution_steps: Only a few cups are solids means some cups are solids and some are not.
Solids lie inside mugs and mugs inside glasses; glasses and water have nothing in common, so no solid is water.
The cups that are solids are therefore never water, so 'some cups can never be water' follows.
common_traps: Reading 'only a few cups are solids' as only 'some cups are solids' still works here, but candidates then miss that part of the cups lie outside solids and make wrong claims about all cups.

short_explanation: Nothing in the statements stops yellow and good from overlapping: good is kept apart only from bright, and yellow is tied only to light. So some yellow being good is possible.

option_rationales.label: a

option_rationales.label: b

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: All bright is light and no good is bright, so the bright part of light can never be good; 'all light being good' is impossible.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: All bright is light, so light certainly contains bright things; 'no light is bright' is false.

solution_steps: No good is bright and all bright is light: the bright part of light can never be good.
Some light is yellow, and yellow may lie in the part of light that is not bright, where good can also sit.
So yellow and good can overlap: 'some yellow being good is a possibility' follows.
common_traps: Treating 'no good is bright' as 'no good is light' wrongly rules out any overlap between good and light-related sets.

short_explanation: All problems are solutions and no solution is written, so no problem can be written. The conclusion follows definitely.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The first statement says some issues are not resolved, so 'all issues are resolved' is false.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Solutions are linked to resolved only through issues, and that link is not fixed, so 'no solution is resolved' is not certain.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Some problems are issues and all problems are solutions, so some solutions are certainly issues. Under the usual exam convention a relation that is already certain is not offered as a mere possibility, so this option is not the intended answer.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Written things have no fixed relation to resolved, so 'some written are not resolved' is not certain.

solution_steps: Only a few problems are issues means some problems are issues and some are not.
All problems are solutions and no solution is written.
Everything inside solutions is kept apart from written, so no problem is written.
common_traps: Marking option d because it is true; it describes a relation that is certain, and the exam convention treats the 'possibility' form as meant for relations that are only possible.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. Another reading set aside: option d is also true on a literal reading, because some solutions are certainly issues and a certain relation is also possible; the key follows the common exam convention that a 'possibility' conclusion is for relations that are not already certain.

short_explanation: 'Only a few voice is audible' means some voice is audible and some voice is not audible. So 'some voice are not audible' follows directly and with certainty.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Good lies inside sound and nothing separates good from audible, so this possibility is in fact open; it is a weaker conclusion than the definite one in option e, which the key accepts.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: All noise is voice, and noise has no fixed relation to sound, so 'some noise is not sound' is not certain.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Audible is linked to sound only through voice, which overlaps both loosely, so 'all audible is sound' is not certain.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Good sits inside sound and only some sound is voice, so good may stay clear of voice; this possibility is also open, but it is weaker than the certain conclusion the key accepts.

solution_steps: 'Only a few voice is audible' contains two parts: some voice is audible, and some voice is not audible.
The second part is exactly option e, so it follows definitely.
common_traps: Reading 'only sound is good' as 'all sound is good'; it means that good things are found only among sound, so all good is sound.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. Other readings set aside: options a and d are also valid possibility conclusions (good lies inside sound and has no fixed relation to audible or voice); the key is the only conclusion that follows with certainty, which is the one accepted.

short_explanation: All sugar is lemon and no lemon is sour, so sugar stays clear of sour. Salt contains all sour but can be larger, and nothing stops the whole of sugar from lying in the part of salt that is not sour. So 'all sugar being salt' is possible.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Some salt is not water, so all salt can never be water.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Some spice is sugar and all sugar is lemon, so some spice is certainly lemon; 'no spice is lemon' is false.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Spice and water are not linked by any chain of statements, so 'some spice are water' is not certain.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Sugar may or may not overlap salt, so 'no sugar is salt' is not certain.

solution_steps: Sugar lies inside lemon, and lemon is kept apart from sour.
Sour lies inside salt, but salt can extend beyond sour.

short_explanation: Statement I alone leaves D on the first, second or third box from the bottom, and statement II alone allows several places too. Together they fix D at the bottom, with G second, C third, F fourth, E fifth and the box named B on top.
explanation_text: Number the boxes from the bottom. Statement I: F is three above D and one box sits between F and G, so D can be first, second or third from the bottom. Statement II: E is immediately below B with more than two boxes between B and D. Together: D on the second or third box would put F on the fifth or top box and leave no room for the pair of E and B with more than two boxes between B and D. So D is at the bottom and F fourth; E and B then take the fifth and top boxes, G the second and C the third.

option_rationales.label: a

From II: E sits immediately below B, and B is at least four boxes away from D.
Combine: only D at the bottom leaves room for both; F is fourth, E fifth, B on top, G second and C third.
So D is the first box from the bottom, and both statements are needed.
key_note: Accepted on a relaxed reading. The question lists the boxes as C, D, E, F, G and H, but statement II speaks of box B; the key follows if B is read as a slip for one of the six boxes (for example H).

short_explanation: Statement I alone fixes the whole building: the second floor has M in Flat 1 and F in Flat 2. Statement II fixes the floors but not the flats, so it cannot say who is in Flat 1 of the second floor.

P is immediately below F and K is immediately above F in the same flat, so P must be on the first floor, F on the second and K on the third, with D on the third too. M is on a floor next to K's, so M is on the second floor, and J, the last person, is on the first floor in Flat 2. P then takes Flat 1 of the first floor, F (not in P's flat number) takes Flat 2 of the second floor, and M is in Flat 1 of the second floor. Statement II gives floors only: F on the first floor, P and D on the second, K and J on the third, M on the first, but it never settles which of P and D is in Flat 1.

option_rationales.label: b

option_rationales.label: c

option_rationales.label: d

solution_steps: From I: D and P are on the first and third floors; P is just below F and F is just below K, so P is on the first floor, F on the second, K and D on the third.
M is next to K's floor, so M is on the second floor; J is on the first floor in Flat 2, so P is in Flat 1.
F is not in P's flat number, so F is in Flat 2 of the second floor and M in Flat 1. Statement I is sufficient.
From II: F on the first floor, K on the third, P on the second, J above P, M below P; P and D share the second floor with no clue for their flats, so II is not sufficient.
common_traps: Treating 'no floor gap' in statement II as 'same floor' instead of 'adjacent floors'; either way II does not fix the flats.

topic_name: Linear row — single row, one direction
short_explanation: Statement II alone gives the row, from left to right, as Q, P, T, V, S, R, so S sits fourth to the right of Q. Statement I allows four different rows and cannot fix S.

S is fourth to the right of Q, so II is sufficient.
From I: rows such as P R S T V Q and R P T V Q S both fit, so I is not sufficient.

short_explanation: Statement II gives a full family: A and K are E's parents, E is married to B's son C, B and H are C's parents, and J is the child of C and E. So K is J's grandfather. Statement I never mentions K, so it cannot answer.

H is J's grandmother but is not A, so H is B's wife and J is a child of B's son and E. Among the seven, B's son must be C, and the only person left to be A's husband is K. The three generations are B, H, A and K; then C and E; then J. So K is J's maternal grandfather. Statement I names B, C, A, E, H and J but says nothing about K.

option_rationales.label: b

H is J's grandmother and is not A, so H is B's wife and J is the child of C and E.
No single parent: A needs a husband in the family, and the only one left is K.
K is the father of E, J's mother, so K is J's grandfather. Statement I never mentions K.

short_explanation: In both examples the first, third and fifth letters move three places forward (B to E, A to D, E to H; G to J, A to D, E to H). Applying that to SOUND gives V, X and G in those places, and VMXLG is the only five-letter option that fits, with O and N each moved two places back.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: VMYLH moves U and D four places forward (Y, H) instead of three (X, G).

Only VMXLG has V, X and G in the first, third and fifth places; its second and fourth letters are O − 2 = M and N − 2 = L.

key_note: Accepted as defensible. The examples do not give one consistent rule for the second and fourth letters (L and M move two forward in BLAME, R and P move seven back in GRAPE, while the key moves O and N two back); the key is the only option matching the consistent +3 rule on the first, third and fifth letters.

First six letters C O M M U N, each two back: A M K K S L.
Last six letters C A T I O N, each two forward: E C V K Q P.
New string A M K K S L I E C V K Q P; K is repeated, so all Ks are removed: A M S L I E C V Q P.
Fourth from the left is L.

short_explanation: Five pairs in 6537189243 have as many digits between them in the number as in the counting series: 6 and 5, 5 and 7, 3 and 1, 8 and 9, and 4 and 3. Five is more than four.

option_rationales.label: d

Digits two apart with one digit between them: 5 and 7 (3 between), 3 and 1 (7 between).
No other pair works, so the count is 5, which is more than four.

short_explanation: J and O meet only through M and L, where J > M ≥ L and L ≤ O. The signs point in opposite directions at L, so O and J have no fixed relation; the same happens between I and N. Neither conclusion is true.

option_rationales.label: b

option_rationales.label: c

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Neither conclusion is certain, so both cannot be true.

O versus J: J > M ≥ L and L ≤ O; the signs change direction at L, so no relation.
I versus N: I > M ≥ L ≤ O > N; again the direction changes at L, so no relation.
common_traps: Reading L ≤ O as if L were above O and chaining straight through.

M ≥ L > I > V, so M > V: I is true.
P > V and B > V; nothing ranks P against B, so II is not certain.

V = Q > R = S < T: the sign turns at S, so V versus T is open: II is not certain.

short_explanation: D and J connect only through C, B and A, where C ≤ D and C = B < A = I ≤ J, so their order is open. For conclusion II, A > B and A = I give I > B, so 'B > I' is false. Neither conclusion is true.

option_rationales.rationale: D > J is not certain: D is above or equal to C, and J is above C by way of A and I, so either may be larger.

D versus J: D ≥ C = B < A = I ≤ J; the signs change at C, so no fixed relation.
B versus I: B < A = I, so B > I is false.

short_explanation: G was born on the 24th of January. Four calendar months later is May, and the person born on the 24th of May is J.

G was born on the 24th of January; four months later on the same date is the 24th of May, which is J.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: C was born on the 24th of March, two months after G.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: D was born on the 7th of May: the right month but a different date from G.

solution_steps: D is three calendar months before E on the same date. Among January, March, May, August and November only May to August and August to November are three months apart.

short_explanation: The inference blames paper demand for tree felling. If most Indian paper mills still use fresh wood pulp rather than recycled paper, rising paper use really does mean more trees cut, which strengthens the link.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Afforestation offsets tree loss; it does not show that paper demand drives deforestation, and if anything softens the concern.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Growth of digital note-taking would reduce paper demand, weakening the inference rather than strengthening it.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Pencils moving away from wood reduces the wood link; it weakens the pencil part of the inference.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Packaging moving to jute and bamboo means less wood-based packaging, which weakens the inference.

common_traps: Picking an option that is about forests in general (like afforestation) rather than one that ties paper demand to tree felling.

short_explanation: 'A mere ___ effort, failing to address deep-rooted malpractices' needs a word for a half-hearted, box-ticking effort: 'perfunctory'. Such a weak report would 'exacerbate' (make worse) the public's worst anxieties about collusion.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 'Meticulous' means careful and thorough, which clashes with 'mere' and 'failing to address', and 'assuage' (calm) clashes with 'worst anxieties'.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 'Redundant' means unnecessary, not shallow, and 'palliate' (soothe) runs against the critical tone.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 'Contentious' means disputed, not superficial, and one does not 'obfuscate' (make unclear) anxieties.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'Dilatory' means causing delay, not shallow; 'vindicate' could suit the second blank, but the first word does not match 'failing to address'.

common_traps: 'Vindicate the public's anxieties' sounds natural, which pulls candidates to option e, but the first blank must describe a shallow effort.

short_explanation: 'Though' sets up a contrast: the measures were first praised as 'proactive' (acting in advance to protect the market) but later proved 'ineffectual' (not working) because they did not stop capital flight.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Measures are not 'hailed' as 'regressive', a negative word.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 'Indispensable' (essential) contradicts 'failing to prevent capital flight'.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 'Hypercritical' means excessively critical of others and cannot describe a failed measure.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'Redundant' means unnecessary, not failing; the sentence says the measures did not work.

common_traps: Missing the contrast signalled by 'Though ... eventually'; the first word must be praise and the second a failure.

short_explanation: If the disclosure was 'sudden and unprompted' and 'poorly synchronized', the motive would be 'debatable' among analysts, and the act itself 'anomalous' (out of the ordinary).

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 'Strategic' clashes with 'unprompted' and 'poorly synchronized'.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: A motive that is 'certain' would not be discussed as uncertain, and 'coordinated' contradicts 'poorly synchronized'.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 'Highly trivial among political analysts' does not make sense; 'impulsive' alone could fit the second blank.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'Transparent' motive and 'premeditated' disclosure contradict 'sudden and unprompted'.

common_traps: 'Impulsive' fits the second blank well, but 'trivial' does not suit 'remains highly ___ among analysts'.

short_explanation: A cross-examination 'so incisive' (sharp and penetrating) would leave the prosecution's arguments 'eviscerated' (gutted, destroyed). The 'so ... that' structure needs a strong cause and a matching result.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 'Scathing' fits the first blank, but 'unassailable' (impossible to attack) is the opposite of the result described.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: A 'superficial' cross-examination would not destroy arguments completely.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: A 'listless' (dull) questioning would not leave arguments 'validated'; that result helps the prosecution.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: A 'convoluted' questioning that 'reinforced' the prosecution does not fit a defence success.

common_traps: 'Scathing' is attractive for the first blank, but the pair must work together and 'unassailable' reverses the meaning.

short_explanation: 'While' sets up a contrast: the manuscript was first celebrated as a 'definitive' (authoritative) account, but carbon-dating raised doubts, forcing researchers to 'scrutinize' (examine closely) its chronological validity.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: A 'spurious' (fake) account would not be celebrated, and doubts would not lead researchers to 'ratify' (approve) it.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 'Tangential' (only loosely related) is not a reason for celebration.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 'Canonical' could suit the first blank, but skepticism leads to checking, not to 'authenticating', which assumes the result is genuine.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: A 'fragmented' account would not be celebrated, and 'disregard' goes further than doubt demands.

common_traps: 'Authenticate' and 'question' both relate to checking, but only 'scrutinize' matches the neutral step skepticism forces, paired with a word of praise.

short_explanation: Only sentence II has an error: 'avoid' takes an '-ing' form directly, so it should be 'barely managed to avoid making', not 'avoid from making'. Sentences I and III are acceptable.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Sentence I is acceptable: a panel that is 'split' is thought of as separate members, so 'them' can refer to them.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Pairs II with I, but I is treated as correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Sentence III is correct: 'cautioned against' and 'persisted in allocating' are the right patterns.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Only II contains an error.

common_traps: 'Avoid from' is a common error carried over from 'prevent from' or 'refrain from'; 'avoid' never takes 'from'.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. Another reading set aside: option c (I and II), if 'The panel ... was ... split, rendering them' is taken as a singular-plural pronoun mismatch; the key treats 'them' as referring to the divided members.

option_rationales.rationale: Both II and III are correct.

option_rationales.label: e

short_explanation: Sentences I and III have errors. In I, destroying a tower with explosives is to 'blow up', not 'blow out' (which means put out a flame). In III, after 'insisted that' the verb takes the base form: 'the executive director resign'. II is correct.
explanation_text: 'Scarcely', 'hardly' and 'barely' at the start of a sentence take the inverted order 'had + subject + past participle' and are followed by 'when', which is exactly what II does. Verbs of demand or insistence such as 'insist', 'demand', 'recommend' and 'suggest' take the base form of the verb in the 'that' clause, whatever the subject: 'insisted that he resign'.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Leaves out III, which also contains an error.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Leaves out I, which also contains an error.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Sentence II is correct: 'Scarcely had ... when' is the right pattern.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Sentence II is correct, so not all three contain errors.

common_traps: Using 'than' after 'scarcely' is the usual error, so candidates who see 'when' should recognise II as correct.

topic_name: Vocabulary from context within a passage
short_explanation: In 'physically accessible but economically prohibitive', 'prohibitive' describes prices so high that people cannot pay them. 'Exorbitant' (far too expensive) is the closest synonym in this sense.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 'Restrictive' fits 'prohibitive' in the sense of rules that forbid, not the price sense used here.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 'Permissive' means allowing, roughly the opposite.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 'Imperative' means essential or urgent, unrelated.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'Inaccessible' describes the effect, but the passage uses 'prohibitive' for the cost itself and has just said the food is 'physically accessible'.

common_traps: 'Inaccessible' looks close, but the sentence contrasts physical access with cost, and 'exorbitant' names the cost.

short_explanation: The passage says monocultural farming 'privileges the overproduction of industrial commodities like corn and soy', and 'this ecological imbalance renders the food supply chain highly fragile to climate-induced anomalies', leading to 'cascading failures in supply elasticity'. Option b says exactly this.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The passage never says corn and soy overproduction protects low-income areas; it says the opposite about fragility.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Retail monopolies are said to abandon rural areas, and this is not linked to corn and soy.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Cost-of-living metrics relate to safety nets, not to crop overproduction.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Nothing in the passage links overproduction to reversing food mirages.

short_explanation: On the safety net itself, the author stresses that it 'relies on antiquated, monolithic bureaucratic metrics that fail to account for acute regional disparities in cost-of-living' and for 'food mirages', which option b captures.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The passage never mentions EBT card fraud.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No drain on agricultural technology budgets is mentioned.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Suburban population spikes are not discussed; suburbs appear only in the retail point.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Meat-packing monopolies are linked to supply chain disruptions, not to the safety net.

short_explanation: 'Precarity' means a state of insecurity and instability, as in 'the precarity of vulnerable households'. Its closest opposite is 'stability'.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 'Vulnerability' is a synonym of precarity, not its opposite.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 'Instability' is a synonym of precarity, not its opposite.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 'Peril' means danger, close in meaning to precarity.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'Resilience' is the ability to recover from shocks, a related idea but not the direct opposite of an insecure condition.

common_traps: The question asks for the opposite; three options are synonyms that catch candidates who read too fast.

short_explanation: Statement I is true: the paradox is the coexistence of food insecurity with 'metabolic syndromes, diabetes, and clinical obesity'. II is true: disruptions caused an 'inflationary spiral' that forced a shift to nutrient-poor food, feeding the paradox. III is false: the passage blames cost, not lack of health awareness. The right choice is I and II, which is option a, not the keyed option b.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes III, which the passage does not support.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: III is not supported; the passage links the food choices to cost and inflation.

key_note: Keyed option b (II and III) includes III, which the passage contradicts: the shift to energy-dense food is 'forcing a regressive substitution' caused by inflation, not ignorance. I and II are both supported, so option a is correct. The option list appears shifted: 'Only (I)' is stuck on the end of the stem, suggesting the original key 'Both (I) and (II)' has moved.

topic_name: Vocabulary from context within a passage
short_explanation: In 'structurally dismantle the entrenched, cyclical dynamics', 'dismantle' means to take apart piece by piece. 'Deconstruct' is the closest in meaning.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 'Obliterate' means wipe out completely, stronger than and different from taking something apart.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 'Subvert' means undermine secretly, which is not the sense here.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 'Reconfigure' means rearrange, not take apart.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'Reinforce' means strengthen, the opposite.

common_traps: 'Obliterate' is tempting because dismantling ends a system, but the word 'structurally' points to taking it apart, not destroying it outright.

short_explanation: The words fit better as 'The prosecutor's scathing analysis ... provided a conclusive link that unravelled the defendant's elaborate corporate fraud scheme.' So the sequence is B, C, A.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Gives 'elaborate analysis', 'conclusive link' and 'scathing fraud scheme'; a fraud scheme is not 'scathing'.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Gives 'conclusive analysis', 'elaborate link' and 'scathing fraud scheme'; a fraud scheme cannot be 'scathing'.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Gives 'elaborate link' and 'conclusive fraud scheme'; a scheme being unravelled is not 'conclusive'.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: As written, 'a scathing link' and 'conclusive fraud scheme' make no sense.

common_traps: 'Elaborate analysis' sounds fine, but then the scheme ends up with a word that cannot describe it.

short_explanation: The sentence should read 'The diplomat's reluctance to sign the treaty ... cost the nation a pivotal strategic alliance in the unfolding geopolitical conflict.' So the sequence is C, B, A.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Keeps 'unfolding to sign', which is not English; a noun is needed before 'to sign'.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Puts 'pivotal' before 'to sign', but an adjective cannot be the subject there.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Gives 'an unfolding strategic alliance' and 'the pivotal geopolitical conflict'; 'pivotal' belongs with the alliance whose loss mattered, and 'unfolding' with the ongoing conflict.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: As written, 'unfolding to sign' and 'the reluctance geopolitical conflict' make no sense.

short_explanation: The sentence should read 'The defence team's astute cross-examination exposed a crucial contradiction that invalidated the key witness's testimony.' So the sequence is B, C, A. Note that 'an astute' becomes 'a crucial' once the words move.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Puts 'crucial' before 'cross-examination' and 'astute' as the verb, but 'astute' is an adjective.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Leaves 'crucial' as the verb after 'that'; a verb like 'invalidated' is needed there.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Keeps 'invalidated cross-examination' and 'astute' as a verb.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: As written, 'crucial the key witness's testimony' has no verb.

common_traps: Only 'invalidated' is a verb, so it must fill the place after 'that'.

short_explanation: The sentence should read 'The team's resilient performance during the financial crisis allowed the firm to navigate market adversity with unwavering focus.' So the sequence is B, C, A.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Gives 'adversity performance' and 'market unwavering', which make no sense.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Gives 'unwavering performance ... navigate market adversity with resilient focus'; this is grammatical, but 'resilient' describes how a team stands up to a crisis and 'unwavering' is the usual word for focus, so the keyed order is the natural one.

short_explanation: Statement I fixes the order Monday to Saturday as S, Q, R, U, T, P, so R went on Wednesday. Statement II allows four different orders, with S, P, Q or R on Wednesday.
explanation_text: Statement I: U went after R and before T, and one person went between R and T, so R, U, T are consecutive with P right after T, and Q right before R. That makes Q, R, U, T, P a block of five days, and S, who went before Q, takes Monday. The order is S, Q, R, U, T, P, so R went on Wednesday. Statement II allows orders such as U P S T R Q, S U P T R Q, T S Q R U P and S T R Q U P, which put S, P, Q and R respectively on Wednesday.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement II alone allows S, P, Q or R on Wednesday.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Statement II alone is not sufficient.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I alone answers the question.

option_rationales.label: e

solution_steps: Statement I: R, U and T fall on consecutive days (one person between R and T, and U between them), with Q the day before R and P the day after T.
That is a block of five: Q, R, U, T, P. S went before Q, so S is Monday.
The order is S, Q, R, U, T, P, so R went on Wednesday. Statement I alone is sufficient.
Statement II allows orders such as U P S T R Q and T S Q R U P, which put different people on Wednesday, so it is not sufficient.

short_explanation: Statement II fixes the order from Chairman down: F, A, B, D, E, C, so B is the General Manager. Statement I allows many orders.
explanation_text: Statement II: only one person is senior to A, so A is Managing Director. B is junior to A and senior to D, and E is immediately junior to D, so the order below A runs B, D, E in that sequence with C not above E. F is senior to C, so F takes the only seat left above A, Chairman, and C is Executive. The order is F (Chairman), A (Managing Director), B (General Manager), D (Senior Manager), E (Assistant Manager), C (Executive). Statement I gives only relative clues and allows 48 orders with anyone as General Manager.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I alone leaves many orders; anyone can be General Manager.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I alone is not sufficient.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Statement II alone answers the question.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Statement II alone is enough; I is not needed.

solution_steps: Statement II: only one person is senior to A, so A is Managing Director.
B is below A and above D, and E is immediately below D; E is not junior to C, so C is Executive.
F is senior to C and the only seat left is Chairman, so F is Chairman, and B, D, E fill General Manager, Senior Manager and Assistant Manager in that order.
B is the General Manager. Statement I gives only relative clues and does not fix any designation.
